title: World Englishes & Global English

pts: Kachru's model distinguishes Inner Circle (English as a primary language), Outer Circle (institutionalised second-language use), and Expanding Circle (foreign-language use) contexts.
This model, though imperfect and debated, remains a widely used starting point for discussing English's global spread.
It reframes 'native speaker' contexts as one circle among several, not the automatic centre.
points.who: Braj Kachru's Three Circles of English

v: Trainee teachers, teachers or DIET faculty
A large drawing of three concentric circles

items: Draw Kachru’s three circles: Inner (for example the UK, USA, Australia), Outer (India, Nigeria, Singapore, Kenya) and Expanding (China, Brazil, Japan, Germany).
Participants write their name on a sticky note and place it where their own English belongs.
Ask: Where would you put a Bengaluru child who speaks English at home? A Kannada-medium learner in a village? A Keralite nurse in the Gulf?
Groups list two strengths and two weaknesses of the model, then meet one alternative, such as Schneider (2007).
With B2+ learners, discuss their own English and ambitions.
Support: provide example countries on cards to place first.
Challenge: redesign the model to account for individual speakers rather than nations.

lines: A: I put myself on the line between Outer and Inner. I think in English sometimes.
B: The model says India is Outer Circle, but my students in Raichur hear English only in school. Their situation is more like Expanding.
T: That is one of the main criticisms: a nation-level model hides the differences inside a country.

blocks.x: The model is best used as a starting point for discussion, not a final classification.

body: Figure 78.1 Three circles, and people between them

Purpose: to show Kachru’s model and its limits. Content: three concentric circles labelled Inner, Outer and Expanding; small figures placed on the boundaries, with question marks. Style: clean diagram, labels as well as colours. Board version: three circles with names on the lines.

items: Padlet (free plan, limited number of boards) or Miro (free plan, limited boards) for virtual sticky notes.

blocks.x: Chalk circles on the board and paper slips.

pts: Indian English, Nigerian English, Singaporean English and others are legitimate, rule-governed varieties, not error-laden deviations from a British or American standard.
This directly extends Unit 59's critique of the single-standard default into a full, positive descriptive framework.
Materials and assessment that treat only Inner Circle varieties as 'correct' misrepresent the actual global linguistic landscape.

v: Twelve sentence cards from Indian English and other varieties

items: Prepare cards with features of Indian English, some of Nigerian or Singapore English, and some genuine learner errors.
Groups sort the cards into ‘variety feature’ and ‘developmental error’, giving reasons.
Share criteria, guiding towards the test: Is it used systematically by proficient speakers in that community?
Discuss when a teacher should point out that a feature differs from other varieties, for example in international exams.
Learners collect expressions from Indian newspapers, signboards and advertisements for a week.
Support: fewer cards, with the variety named on each.
Challenge: find the same meaning expressed in British, American and Indian English.

lines: Please do the needful. (Indian English: established in official correspondence)
He is my cousin-brother. (Indian English: clarifies gender and relationship)
We will prepone the meeting. (Indian English: useful lexical innovation)
She go to school yesterday. (developmental error: not systematic among proficient users)
I am knowing the answer. (Indian English feature in informal speech; marked in many other varieties)
S1: How can ‘I am knowing’ be correct if the exam marks it wrong?
T: It is regular in some Indian English speech. For the exam, you need the other form too. Knowing both is a skill.

blocks.x: Descriptions of Indian English document features like these at the levels of sounds, grammar, vocabulary and discourse (Sailaja 2009).

body: Purpose: to distinguish variety features from developmental errors. Content: two baskets labelled ‘community norm’ and ‘still developing’, with sentence cards falling into each. Style: friendly. Board version: two columns with a line between.

items: Google Books Ngram Viewer (free) to see how often an expression appears in published books over time; it does not separate Indian English, so use it only as a rough guide.

blocks.x: Cuttings from local English newspapers pasted into a class scrapbook.

pts: ELF research studies English specifically as used between non-native speakers, often with no native speaker present at all.
This is distinct from World Englishes, which studies established national varieties — ELF studies English in transient, cross-cultural use.
This connects directly to Tier I's Lingua Franca Core (Unit 4), grounding it in a fuller research field.

v: A short recording or transcript of two non-native speakers using English together

items: Play a short exchange between, for example, an Indian and a Korean speaker negotiating a delivery date.
Learners note where the speakers had difficulty and how they solved it: repetition, rephrasing, slowing down, checking.
Pairs role-play a similar exchange, using one strategy on purpose.
Discuss how this differs from imitating a native speaker.
Without a recording, two adults act out a scripted exchange.
Support: give a list of strategies to tick while listening.
Challenge: learners transcribe one repair sequence and explain it.

blocks.x: A lingua franca exchange (written for this book):

lines: A: We need the parts by the twenty… twenty-fifth.
B: Twenty-five? Of March?
A: Yes, twenty-five March. Is it possible?
B: Twenty-five is difficult. Twenty-eight, maybe?
A: Twenty-eight is OK. Please confirm by email.
Strategies: repetition of key numbers, confirmation check, simplified syntax, a request for written confirmation.

blocks.x: ELF research focuses on how speakers achieve understanding in exchanges like this, often through accommodation and co-operation, rather than on how far each speaker is from a native model (Seidlhofer 2011). World Englishes research, by contrast, describes the established varieties of particular communities.

body: Purpose: to distinguish World Englishes from ELF. Content: left, a map of national varieties asking ‘What are this community’s norms?’; right, two speakers joined by a bridge asking ‘How do they make it work?’. Style: parallel panels. Board version: two boxes with one question each.

items: VOICE (Vienna-Oxford International Corpus of English; free online access for research and teaching) for transcripts of ELF interaction. [VERIFY current access and terms]

blocks.x: A scripted exchange read aloud by two learners.

body: ELF corpora record features that recur across many speakers without loss of understanding, such as dropping the third-person -s (she look). Researchers disagree about what this means for teaching (Seidlhofer 2011; Jenkins 2015).

pts: Unit 4's Lingua Franca Core, prioritising intelligibility over native-like accent, follows directly from this research field's findings.
ELF research has identified which specific phonological features most affect intelligibility between non-native speakers.
This is one of the clearest, most practically actionable applications of World Englishes and ELF theory.

v: A list of pronunciation features; minimal-pair cards

items: Show two lists: features in Jenkins’s Lingua Franca Core (most consonants, vowel length, consonant clusters at the start of words, nuclear stress) and features outside it (the th sounds, weak forms, exact vowel quality).
Learners test themselves in pairs with minimal pairs from the Core list: ship/sheep, play/pay, spot/pot.
Pairs choose one Core feature they find difficult and practise it.
Plan a five-minute weekly pronunciation slot built on these priorities (Unit 4).
Add a feature that matters for your learners’ first languages, for example the /v/–/w/ contrast for speakers of some Indian languages.
Support: pictures for each minimal pair.
Challenge: learners record themselves and a partner judges intelligibility.

lines: I said SPOT, not POT. (initial cluster: in the Core)
Please SIT here / Please SEAT here. (vowel length: in the Core)
I THINK / I TINK. (th sound: outside the Core; usually understood in context)
T: Which of these could cause a real misunderstanding?
S1: Spot and pot. And sit and seat.
S2: ‘Tink’ is fine. Everybody knows ‘I tink’.

blocks.x: Jenkins (2000) proposed that pronunciation teaching for international use should prioritize the Core features and treat others as less urgent. The Core itself has since been debated and refined.

body: Figure 78.4 What matters most for being understood

Purpose: to show pronunciation priorities. Content: a target with the Core features near the centre (vowel length, initial clusters, nuclear stress, most consonants) and non-Core features in the outer ring (th sounds, weak forms, vowel quality). Style: clean target. Board version: two concentric circles with labels.

items: YouGlish (free with advertisements) for hearing words in real contexts from speakers of many varieties.
Forvo (free for listening) for pronunciations of individual words by speakers from many countries.

pts: Most major exams still assess against a single, typically Inner Circle standard, raising genuine questions about fairness and construct validity.
This connects to Unit 57's washback work — the standard-variety choice is itself a validity question.
Some assessment bodies are beginning to more explicitly recognise plural standards, though this remains contested and evolving.

v: Sample items from a board or international examination

items: Collect ten sample items from an examination your learners take.
For each item, ask: Would an item answer that is correct in Indian English be marked wrong?
Discuss whether each marked item measures communicative ability or knowledge of one variety.
Link to Units 57 and 73: suggest one change that would improve the item’s validity for your learners.
Compare a state board’s marking guidelines with an international test’s on spelling variation.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Items and comments (written for this book):

lines: Choose the correct word: We live in a (flat / apartment). Both are correct in different varieties. The item tests variety, not competence.
Correct the error: I am having a car. The key says I have. Fair for a formal written test that specifies a standard; the specification should say so.
A: We cannot change the board’s marking, but we can explain why the exam needs the standard form without telling learners their English is wrong.

blocks.x: Canagarajah (2006) argued that assessment should respond to the needs of English as an international language, including the ability to negotiate between varieties. The choice of a standard is a validity question, not just a matter of taste.

body: Purpose: to show variety bias in test keys. Content: a multiple-choice item with two correct answers from different varieties; the key ticks only one; a question mark hovers over the other. Style: clear. Board version: an item written out with two ticks and one crossed out.

items: Google Forms (free) to build a shared bank of reviewed items with comments.

blocks.x: A paper item review sheet with three columns.

pts: Course design should make a deliberate, informed choice about which variety or varieties to teach and expose learners to.
Exposing learners to multiple varieties, even while teaching one as a primary model, better reflects real-world English use.
This connects directly to Unit 24's avoidance of the single-culture trap, now applied specifically to linguistic variety.

v: Your scheme of work (Unit 14); a list of audio sources in several varieties

items: Write down the variety you currently use as your model. Is it a deliberate choice?
List your learners’ likely future uses of English and choose a primary model that fits them.
Plan exposure to at least three other varieties across a term, using listening texts, reading and guests.
Add these to the scheme of work. This extends the single-culture caution of Unit 24.
In a DIET course, trainees plan a variety-exposure strand for one class across a year.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A teacher’s plan (written for this book):

lines: Primary model: Educated Indian English for speaking and writing; standard British spelling for board examinations.
Exposure plan: Term 1 – a Nigerian short story; an Australian podcast clip. Term 2 – a Singaporean news clip; a British radio interview. Term 3 – a video call with a pen-pal school in another state.
Classroom language: ‘This word is used in Indian English. In British English people say… Both are fine; choose to suit your listener.’

blocks.x: Matsuda (2003) proposed that learners be taught one variety as a model while being exposed to others, so that they learn about English as an international language as well as learning it.

body: Purpose: to show a primary model with wider exposure. Content: a learner at a desk with one open book labelled ‘teaching model’ and a window behind showing several speakers from different countries. Style: warm. Board version: a box labelled ‘model’ and a window with speech bubbles.

items: BBC Learning English (free) and Voice of America Learning English (free) for audio in two Inner Circle varieties.
All India Radio and Doordarshan news archives on YouTube (free) for Indian English broadcasting.

blocks.x: The teacher reads texts from different varieties aloud, and invites local English speakers from different backgrounds to speak to the class.

pts: Learners sometimes hold strong preferences for a specific 'standard' variety, shaped by prestige associations worth understanding, not dismissing.
This connects to Unit 59's identity work — variety choice can carry real identity and aspiration significance for learners.
Respecting learner preference while also broadening genuine awareness of global variety is a real, ongoing pedagogical balance.

v: A short attitude questionnaire; three short audio clips

items: Play three clips: an Indian English, a British English and an American English speaker reading the same short text.
Learners rate each on scales: clear, friendly, educated, I would like to speak like this.
Chart the results and discuss: What do we associate with each accent?
Learners write one sentence about the English they want to speak and why. Accept all answers.
Use it as an action-research baseline (Unit 67) and repeat it at the end of term.
Support: smiley-face scales.
Challenge: learners design two questions to add to the survey.

lines: Educated: British 4.3, American 4.0, Indian 3.1 (out of 5).
Clear: Indian 4.5, British 3.6, American 3.8.
I want to speak like this: British 3.9, American 4.1, Indian 3.0.
S1: I want British accent because it is posh. Job interviews also.
S2: But the Indian one was easiest to understand.
T: Both of those are good reasons. Can you want a clear, confident Indian English and still understand British English well?

blocks.x: Attitude research has found strong attachment to native-speaker accents even among proficient users of English (Jenkins 2007). Such preferences reflect real social pressures, so the teacher’s job is to understand them and widen learners’ choices, not to dismiss them. Unit 59 examines language and identity in more depth.

body: Figure 78.7 What an accent seems to say

Purpose: to show language attitudes. Content: three speakers, each with a bar chart above of ratings for ‘clear’, ‘friendly’ and ‘educated’, showing different patterns. Style: simple chart. Board version: three small bar charts.

items: Google Forms (free) or Mentimeter (free plan) for the rating scale.

blocks.x: A paper rating sheet and a hand tally.

body: Avoid using the word ‘correct’ when a learner prefers a particular accent. Use ‘appropriate’, ‘clear’ or ‘suitable for this listener’ instead. The change in language helps learners separate what is intelligible from what is prestigious.

pts: Understand and represent English's genuine global plurality, while still making practical, informed choices about classroom teaching targets.
This is not a call to teach every variety simultaneously, but to avoid presenting one variety as the only legitimate form.
This theoretical grounding directly informs the decolonising-ELT and native-speaker-myth work closing out this series.

items: Write a short statement (100–150 words) of your stance on variety in English teaching.
Include your teaching model, your exposure plan, your response to Indian English features and your exam preparation.
A partner looks for contradictions; revise.
Return to it after reading Units 96 and 98.
In a school, draft a shared statement for the English department.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: A sample stance (written for this book):

lines: I teach an educated Indian English as my speaking model, and standard written English for exams. I expose my learners to at least three other varieties each term. I do not treat established Indian English features as errors in speaking, but I show learners where they differ from other varieties, so that they can choose. I prepare them for the exam’s expectations and explain why those expectations exist.

blocks.x: This is descriptive pluralism with practical choice: English is described as plural, and teaching makes informed decisions within that plurality (Kirkpatrick 2007).

body: Purpose: to show the working stance. Content: a wide funnel at the top containing many variety labels, narrowing to a single path labelled ‘my teaching model’, with side windows labelled ‘exposure’. Style: clean. Board version: a funnel with labels.

items: Google Docs (free) for drafting and sharing stance statements.

blocks.x: A handwritten stance statement in the teaching journal.

body: For one week, keep a list of every time you correct a learner’s English. At the end of the week, mark each correction as ‘developmental error’ or ‘variety feature’. Did you correct any variety features? Decide what you will do differently.

dek: Unit 78 of 100: English today is plural — legitimate national and regional varieties, not one standard with deviations elsewhere. A full descriptive and pedagogical framework.

aims.x: Unit 74 introduced English as a pluricentric language in the classroom. This unit examines the theory and research behind that position: Kachru’s three circles, World Englishes as legitimate varieties, and the separate field of English as a lingua franca (ELF). It follows the implications into pronunciation, assessment, the choice of a teaching model and learners’ attitudes, and ends with a working stance a teacher can defend.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe Kachru’s three circles and summarize the main criticisms of the model;
explain why established varieties such as Indian English are described as rule-governed rather than error-laden;
distinguish World Englishes research from ELF research;
relate ELF findings on intelligibility to pronunciation priorities;
identify the validity questions raised when tests assume a single standard;
make and justify a choice of teaching model while exposing learners to other varieties;
respond respectfully to learners’ preferences for a prestige variety;
state a working stance of descriptive pluralism and practical choice.

why: Why this matters. Tier I's Lingua Franca Core and Tier III's critical language awareness both gestured at this. This poster gives the full picture that grounds both.

background.x: For much of the twentieth century, ELT assumed a single target: the English of an educated British or American native speaker. From the late 1970s, Braj Kachru, an Indian-born linguist working in the United States, argued that English in India, Nigeria, Singapore and elsewhere had developed its own norms through long use in education, administration, law and literature, and should be described on its own terms (Kachru 1985, 1992).

His three-circle model showed that most users of English were outside the Inner Circle. Critics note that it is organized by nation rather than by speaker, that it cannot easily place multilingual individuals or countries such as South Africa, and that it still puts the Inner Circle at the centre (Jenkins 2015). Later models, such as Schneider’s (2007) dynamic model of postcolonial Englishes, describe how varieties develop through stages from foundation to differentiation.

A second field, English as a lingua franca (ELF), grew from the late 1990s. Jennifer Jenkins (2000) studied intelligibility between non-native speakers and proposed a Lingua Franca Core of pronunciation features; Barbara Seidlhofer (2011) and colleagues built ELF corpora such as VOICE and studied how speakers accommodate to each other.

India is central to this story. Indian English has a long written tradition, a descriptive literature (for example Sailaja 2009), and millions of users who use it alongside other languages. NEP 2020 and NCF 2023 emphasize multilingualism and the home language as a resource (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). A teacher who treats every Indian English feature as a mistake is not only being unkind but misdescribing the language. This unit gives the theoretical grounding for Units 4, 59 and 74, and prepares for the native-speaker and decolonizing discussions of Units 96 and 98.

items: Model critique. A short written evaluation of Kachru’s model, with two strengths, two weaknesses and one alternative.
Feature analysis. A sorted set of sentences separating variety features from developmental errors, with criteria.
Test review. A review of ten examination items for variety bias, with suggested changes.
Stance statement. A 100–150 word working stance, with its teaching model and exposure plan.
Which variety of English did you grow up treating as ‘correct’? Why?
How do you respond when a learner uses an Indian English expression in class?
What do your learners want from English, and how do their goals affect your choice of model?
How far do the examinations your learners take reflect the English they will actually use?
What would change in your classroom if you took the ELF findings on intelligibility seriously?

perm: All sentence cards, transcripts, test items, class results and stance statements are written for this book; the survey results describe a fictional class. Jenkins (2007), English as a Lingua Franca: Attitude and Identity (Oxford University Press), is cited in the text and should be added to the consolidated bibliography. Extracts from VOICE or other corpora must follow their terms of use. Audio clips from BBC, VOA, All India Radio or YouTube should be played from source rather than reproduced. Screenshots of Padlet, Miro, YouGlish, Forvo, Google Ngram Viewer or Google Forms require permission or replacement with original illustrations.

terms.def: (1) An adjustment to how a learner accesses a task or test, such as extra time or enlarged print, which changes the route but not the destination. (2) In ELF talk, adjusting one’s speech to be understood by a listener.

English used as a shared language between speakers who have different first languages, such as an Indian and a Japanese engineer. Research focuses on mutual intelligibility rather than conformity to native-speaker norms (Seidlhofer 2011).
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English has no historical or official role but is widely learned as a foreign language, such as China, Japan and Brazil (Kachru 1985).
The variety of English used in India, with its own features of pronunciation, vocabulary and grammar, such as prepone or co-brother. It is a legitimate variety of English in its own right.
In Kachru’s model of World Englishes, countries where English is the primary language of most people, such as the UK, the USA and Australia (Kachru 1985).
The extent to which a speaker’s words can be understood by listeners. Many teachers now aim for international intelligibility rather than a native-speaker accent (Jenkins 2000).
People’s beliefs and feelings about languages, varieties and accents, such as prestige attached to certain accents, which affect how speakers are judged and how learners feel.

A set of pronunciation features, identified by Jennifer Jenkins (2000), that appear most important for intelligibility when English is used between non-native speakers, such as most consonant sounds and nuclear stress.

In Kachru’s (1985) model of world Englishes, the countries, such as India, Nigeria and Singapore, where English was established through colonial history and has official or institutional roles alongside other languages.

The varieties of English used around the world, such as Indian, Nigerian and Singaporean English, each seen as legitimate with its own norms. The concept is closely associated with Kachru’s Three Circles model.
